case_studies.title: AutoSpec: Safety Rule Evolution for LLM Agents via Inductive Logic Programming
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate complex tasks by integrating language models with external tools and environments. However, their autonomy poses significant safety risks: agents may execute destructive commands, leak sensitive data, or violate domain constraints. Existing safety approaches face a fundamental tradeoff: hand-crafted rules are interpretable but brittle, with overly conservative rules blocking safe operations (high false positives) while permissive rules miss unsafe behaviors (high false negatives). case_studies.summary: This research aims to solve the problem of safety risks in large language model agents by creating a system called AutoSpec, which uses inductive logic programming to evolve safety rules. AutoSpec's result is a more balanced approach to safety rules, reducing false positives and false negatives. This research focuses on improving the safety of LLM agents, which may not directly impact cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving the safety of large language model agents rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper describes a novel approach to safety rule evolution for LLM agents, using Inductive Logic Programming. This directly affects how IT engineers work with large language models, especially in automating complex tasks.

case_studies.title: Detecting AI Coding Agents in Open Source: A Validated Multi-Method Census of 180 Million Repositories
case_studies.abstract: Generative AI coding agents are entering the open-source supply chain, yet their diverse and often invisible traces leave their prevalence poorly understood. We introduce a multi-layered detection framework that integrates configuration-file scanning, commit-message analysis, author-identity matching, and bot-signature lookup across World of Code (180M+ Git repositories), classifying agent traces into four behavioral types. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of detecting AI coding agents in open-source code by building a multi-layered detection framework, which resulted in identifying over 850,000 AI-generated code commits. The framework analyzes configuration files, commit messages, and author identities to detect AI agent traces. This research helps understand the prevalence of AI coding agents in open-source code.

case_studies.title: Neglected Free Lunch from Post-training: Progress Advantage for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Process reward models enable fine-grained, step-level evaluation of LLMs, yet building them for agentic settings remains prohibitively difficult: long-horizon interactions, irreversible actions, and stochastic environment feedback make both human annotation and Monte Carlo estimation infeasible at scale. In this work, we show that reinforcement learning (RL) post-training already provides the ingredients for effective step-level scoring, eliminating the need for dedicated reward model training altogether. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of building process reward models for large language models (LLMs) by using reinforcement learning post-training, which eliminates the need for dedicated reward model training. The researchers built a method to derive an implicit advantage from stochastic Markov decision processes. The result is a more efficient way to evaluate LLMs in agentic settings.

case_studies.title: To Isolate or to Score? Model-Adaptive Assessment for Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent RAG
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent document assessment for retrieval-augmented generation is computationally expensive, driving practitioners toward smaller, deployable models whose assessment mechanisms remain poorly understood. We conduct a controlled study of training-free interventions on 7B-9B instruction-tuned models across diverse QA benchmarks, revealing a sharp dichotomy in how models benefit from assessment. For weaker baselines, the dominant mechanism is per-document isolation. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of costly multi-agent document assessment for retrieval-augmented generation by introducing a model-adaptive assessment method. The team built and tested a new approach on large language models, finding that simpler 'isolation' methods can be just as effective as full assessment in some cases. The result shows potential for cost savings in certain AI model deployments.

case_studies.title: RAVEN: Long-Horizon Reasoning & Navigation with a Visuo-Spatio-Temporal Memory
case_studies.abstract: Long-term robot deployment requires a compact and scalable memory that preserves fine-grained visual semantics, grounds observations in space and time, and enables efficient storage and retrieval. In this paper, we propose RAVEN, an agentic memory system for long-horizon robotic question answering and navigation. RAVEN stores visual embeddings with pose and time in a vector database, and grounds retrieval in a spatial map to answer queries and navigate to goals. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of long-term robot navigation by creating a memory system called RAVEN that stores visual semantics and enables efficient storage and retrieval. The researchers built RAVEN, which uses a vector database and spatial map to answer queries and navigate to goals. The result is a compact and scalable memory system for long-horizon robotic question answering and navigation.

case_studies.title: RevengeBench: Reverse Engineering Code-Space Policies from Behavioral Experiments
case_studies.abstract: For most of scientific history, researchers studying behavior could only infer hidden mechanisms from outward actions: an inverse problem that becomes more tractable when observation is augmented by targeted intervention. We pose a computational analogue: given only behavioral traces of an agent in a game environment, can a learner reconstruct the underlying decision program as executable code, and how much does this reconstruction improve with the ability to design controlled experiments? We introduce RevengeBench, a benchmark of 75 LLM generated, Elo-calibrated policies across five game envi
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of reverse engineering code-space policies from behavioral experiments by introducing RevengeBench, a benchmark of 75 policies across five game environments, resulting in improved reconstruction of underlying decision programs. The team built a computational model to reconstruct executable code from agent behavior in game environments. This research is not directly relevant to cloud infrastructure management.
